title: How do you calculate payback and NPV in a case interview, step by step?
description: Worked examples of payback and simple NPV for investment cases, with discount factors to remember and how to explain the result.
hook: Investment cases often end with the question "is it worth it?" Payback gives a quick answer; NPV gives a better one. Here are both worked through with numbers you could do on paper.
body:
Payback

A new machine costs £1M and saves £300k a year. Payback = 1,000 ÷ 300 ≈ 3.3 years. If the client wants payback within four years, it passes.

Simple NPV

The same machine lasts five years, and the client's cost of capital is 10%. Discount factors to remember at 10%: year 1 ≈ 0.91, year 2 ≈ 0.83, year 3 ≈ 0.75, year 4 ≈ 0.68, year 5 ≈ 0.62. Together they add to about 3.79.

Present value of savings: £300k × 3.79 ≈ £1.14M. NPV = £1.14M − £1M = about +£140k. Positive, so the investment creates value.

When payback misleads

Project A pays back in 2 years but lasts 3. Project B pays back in 3 years but lasts 10. Payback prefers A; NPV will usually prefer B. Always compare payback with the asset's life.

How to say it

It pays back in just over three years, within the target, and over its five-year life it creates about £140k of value after allowing for a 10% cost of capital.

More background in the time value of money explained.
